title: Processes and Threads
description: Understand how the OS manages processes and threads, the real cost of context switches, and why thread safety is the source of most production concurrency bugs.

segments.text: Let's talk about something most engineers take for granted: processes and threads. You use them every day, but understanding what actually happens during a context switch separates senior engineers from everyone else.

A process is an isolated execution environment. It gets its own virtual address space, typically four gigabytes on 32-bit systems, or 128 terabytes on 64-bit Linux. It has its own page table, file descriptor table, and signal handlers. Complete isolation.

Virtual memory is the magic that makes this work. Each process thinks it has contiguous memory, but the MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames. The TLB caches these translations. A TLB miss costs roughly 10 to 100 nanoseconds, and a full page table walk can cost 200 nanoseconds on modern hardware.

When the OS switches between processes, it saves all CPU registers, flushes the TLB, swaps the page table pointer, and restores the new process state. This costs roughly one to five microseconds of direct CPU time, but the real killer is indirect: your L1, L2, and L3 caches go cold.

Think about this carefully. If a context switch costs five microseconds directly, and cache warming costs another ten to fifty microseconds in practice, what happens when you have a thousand threads on a four-core machine?
segments.thought_prompt: How many context switches per second would 1000 threads on 4 cores cause? What's the overhead?

segments.text: Threads exist inside a process and share the same address space, the same heap, and the same file descriptors. Creating a thread is roughly ten times cheaper than forking a process because you skip page table duplication. On Linux, clone with CLONE_VM takes about ten microseconds versus a hundred for fork.

Each thread needs its own stack, typically eight megabytes on Linux by default. Do the math: 32,000 threads times eight megabytes equals 256 gigabytes of virtual memory just for stacks. In practice, Linux starts thrashing well before that. I've seen production Java services die at around 10,000 threads because the scheduler overhead alone consumed 30 percent of CPU.

Here's where shared memory becomes dangerous. Two threads incrementing the same counter without synchronization is a data race. The CPU does read, modify, write as separate steps. If two threads interleave, you lose updates. Instagram hit exactly this bug at scale: their like counter was losing roughly one in every ten thousand likes.

Consider this production scenario: your web server uses a shared in-memory cache with a HashMap. Under load, two threads call put simultaneously, triggering a resize. On the old JDK, this caused infinite loops due to linked list corruption. Not a theoretical problem — it took down services at Amazon.
segments.thought_prompt: What data structure properties make a HashMap particularly dangerous under concurrent writes?

segments.text: Linux treats threads and processes almost identically internally. Both are tasks represented by a task_struct. The difference is just which resources are shared. This is why Linux's clone syscall has flags: CLONE_VM for shared memory, CLONE_FILES for shared file descriptors. Threads are just processes that share more.

In production, here's the rule of thumb: use processes for isolation — microservices, sandboxing, crash containment. Use threads when you need shared memory and low-latency communication. Use async I/O when you're I/O-bound with thousands of concurrent connections. Node.js and Go chose option three for very good reasons.

Remember: a context switch isn't just saving registers. It's blowing away your cache locality, flushing TLB entries, and burning microseconds that add up fast. Understanding this cost is why Netflix tunes their thread pools obsessively and why Google moved to userspace threading with Fibers.
